title: Google DeepMind releases EmbeddingGemma 2 — a 740M multimodal open embedding model
subtitle: The Apache 2.0 release maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a shared 768-dimensional space and runs the full quantized stack on roughly 567 MB of RAM.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Google DeepMind published EmbeddingGemma 2 on October 6, releasing the 740-million-parameter multimodal embedding model under the Apache 2.0 license on Hugging Face and Kaggle. The release maps text, code, images, video, and audio into a shared 768-dimensional vector space, which lets a text query retrieve a matching audio or video segment directly, without a transcription step in between. The composition is modular: a 270M-parameter text component, an optional 170M-parameter vision encoder, and an optional 300M-parameter audio encoder, so a developer can load only the encoders a specific task needs. Google reports the full quantized stack running at roughly 567 MB of active RAM on a Pixel 11 Pro, with the text-only configuration dropping to 191 MB.

The design decisions matter more than the parameter count. First-generation EmbeddingGemma, released in September 2025, was a text-only 308M-parameter model specifically pitched for on-device use. EmbeddingGemma 2 keeps the on-device budget — half a gigabyte for the full multimodal stack is small enough to fit alongside a reasonable application model on a current phone — while adding four more modalities and a Matryoshka-style design that exposes smaller usable dimensions at 512, 256, and 128. The 8,192-token context window and shared embedding space are the practical pieces: they turn the model into a retrieval primitive that applications can call locally against mixed-media data.

The strategic context is that embeddings are quietly the most-deployed piece of modern AI. Every retrieval-augmented generation system, every semantic search box, every on-device photo search, every voice-note transcript lookup leans on an embedding model behind the scenes. Those models have mostly been English-centric, text-only, and either closed (OpenAI, Cohere) or awkward to run on a phone (large open models). An Apache 2.0, multimodal, half-a-gig-of-RAM model from DeepMind takes a large category of applications off the API bill and off the data-leaves-the-device risk register. Google's framing — that deployers remain responsible for application-level safeguards — is a reminder that "on-device" does not mean "consequence-free."

A takeaway for learners: when you read about a new model, scan for three numbers that are not benchmarks. The license (what you are allowed to do with the weights), the memory footprint (where you can run it), and the dimensionality of the output (how much vector-database storage every embedding will cost you). Those three decide whether a model is a tool you can actually build on or an interesting paper. EmbeddingGemma 2's Apache 2.0, 567 MB, 768-dimension profile is a sentence worth memorizing — it is what a serious on-device retrieval model looks like in late 2026.
